h1: SEO for dental clinics: win the map pack or stay invisible
metaTitle: SEO for Dental Clinics: Map Pack and Reviews
metaDescription: SEO for dental clinics that lives in the map pack. We fix your Google Business Profile, build compliant review velocity and rank treatment pages locally.
answer: For a single-location dental clinic the map pack is the whole game — three listings above the organic results, ranked on relevance, distance and prominence. Reviews are the prominence lever you control. A clinic adding eight fresh reviews a month tends to beat one sitting on 400 reviews from 2021 inside the same 3 km ring.
takeaways: You are not competing with every dentist in the city. You're competing with the dozen inside your patients' walking-and-parking radius, and the ranking set changes every few hundred metres.
**Review velocity beats review count.** A steady eight a month with replies outperforms a big stale pile, and it's the one signal a small clinic can genuinely out-work a chain on.
Photo geotagging does nothing. Google strips EXIF on upload. Every agency still selling it as a local ranking tactic is billing you for a myth.
Treatment pages win on the numbers people actually search: cost band, number of sittings, and what it feels like. Not on 'we use the latest technology'.
Two clinics 1.5 km apart will filter each other out of the same map pack. Plan the second branch's catchment before you sign the lease, not after.

sections.h2: Three slots, and one of them is a proximity accident
body: Google names three things for local ranking: relevance, distance and prominence. It doesn't publish the weights, and anyone who tells you the exact percentages is guessing with confidence. What is observable, every day, in any Indian city: distance dominates for `dentist near me`, and content cannot overcome geography.

So stop trying. Your realistic catchment for near-me searches is roughly the 2–3 km ring around your chair, tighter in dense areas like Andheri or Koramangala and wider in low-density outskirts. Inside that ring you should be in the three-pack for the treatments you actually do. Outside it, you should be chasing a different query shape entirely.

That second query shape is the locality name. `dentist in indiranagar`, `dental clinic near hsr layout`, `root canal specialist in vashi` — these behave more like ordinary local search, they carry a wider effective radius, and they reward an actual page on your site rather than just a profile.

callout.title: The keyword-in-the-name trick
callout.body: Renaming your Google profile to 'Smile Dental Clinic — Best Dentist in Whitefield, Implants & Braces' does move rankings, briefly. It also breaks Google's naming guideline, and it's the single most-reported violation in local search. A competitor files one edit and your listing gets stripped or suspended. It is not worth it.

sections.h2: Review velocity, without getting your profile suspended
body: This is the lever, and most clinics pull it wrongly once and then give up. Reviews feed prominence, and freshness matters because a review from four years ago tells Google nothing about whether the clinic is still good. A clinic that adds a handful every month, with replies, keeps signalling.

The system that works is boring and operational, which is why agencies rarely sell it: the review is requested at the chair, by name, at the moment the treatment finishes and the patient is relieved. Not by SMS three days later.

Against Google policy, and India now has a BIS standard (IS 19000:2022) on online consumer reviews plus active CCPA scrutiny of paid reviews.

Free, visible to patients comparing three clinics, and it keeps the profile active.

subs.h3: The compliance bit dentists actually have to care about
body: Dentists in India sit under the Dentists Act, 1948 and the Dental Council of India's ethics code — now moving to the National Dental Commission created by the National Dental Commission Act, 2023 — not the NMC that governs physicians. The principle is the same either way: soliciting patients and self-advertising are restricted, factual information is not.

Practically, that means you may ask for feedback and publish it. You may not write it, buy it, or reply in a way that discloses clinical detail. 'Glad the implant settled well, Mr Sharma' publishes a patient's treatment to the internet. Keep replies warm and non-specific.

sections.h2: The Google Business Profile fields that move rankings
body: Most clinics fill in the name, address, phone and one photo, then wonder why the chain three streets away outranks them. The [Google Business Profile](/glossary/google-business-profile) has roughly a dozen fields that do real work, and they take an afternoon.
bullets: **Primary category.** 'Dentist', 'Dental Clinic', 'Dental Implants Periodontist', 'Orthodontist', 'Cosmetic Dentist' and 'Pediatric Dentist' surface for different searches. Pick the one matching your highest-value treatment, then add the rest as secondaries.
**Services**, each with a written description. This is a free relevance signal and almost nobody completes it.
**Photos of the actual clinic** — exterior from the road, waiting area, chair, sterilisation setup, the team. Sterilisation photos convert in India specifically, because it's the unspoken worry.
**Hours, including a real Sunday policy**, plus holiday hours. A wrong 'open now' costs you the walk-in and earns you a one-star.
**The booking link**, pointed at a page that loads in under two seconds on a mid-range Android on 4G.
**Attributes** — wheelchair accessible entrance, women-led, restroom, parking — which feed filters patients actually use.
**Q&A seeded by you** with the real questions: does it hurt, do you take EMI, is the implant cost inclusive of the crown.

callout.title: Two myths to stop paying for
callout.body: Geotagged photos do nothing — Google strips EXIF data on upload. And bulk citation submissions to 300 random directories stopped mattering years ago. What still matters is that your name, address and phone match exactly across Google, Practo, Justdial, Apple Maps and Bing Places. Consistency, not volume.

sections.h2: Treatment pages: implants, aligners, root canals
body: The map pack brings the near-me searches. Treatment pages bring the researched, high-value ones — and in dentistry the value gap between a scaling appointment and a full-arch implant case is enormous, so this is where the money is.

Every one of these queries is really a cost query wearing a clinical hat. `dental implant cost in india`, `invisalign cost bangalore`, `root canal price near me`, `braces vs aligners which is better`. Publishing a price band is uncomfortable. It is also the query, and the clinic that answers it gets the call while the one hiding behind 'consult us for pricing' gets skipped.
numbered: **A real price band with a stated reason for the range.** 'Single implant, ₹25,000–₹60,000 depending on the implant system and whether you need a bone graft' answers the question and pre-qualifies the caller. Add a review date and keep it current.
**Number of sittings and total elapsed time.** For implants and aligners the timeline drives the decision more than the price does.
**What it actually feels like**, honestly, including the day-two discomfort. Patients trust the clinic that mentions it.
**Who is not a candidate.** The strongest trust signal on any treatment page, and the cheapest to write.
**The alternative you'd suggest instead**, with its price. Losing a case you'd have lost anyway costs nothing; being the clinic that said so wins the referral.

body: Aligner and implant brands are trademarks. Write about them factually — 'we work with clear aligner systems including X' — and don't imply certification or provider status you don't hold. If you are a certified provider, say so and link the verification. That's a genuine differentiator most clinics forget to claim.

sections.h2: Two clinics, one map pack: how multi-location actually behaves
body: Google generally shows one listing per business per query. Open a second clinic 1.5 km from the first and they don't double your coverage — they filter each other, and you've spent a fit-out to fight yourself. Open one in a genuinely separate catchment and you get two independent three-pack chances.
Where a second location does work, the setup is mechanical and most groups get it wrong.
bullets: **A separate profile per clinic**, with its own phone number and its own staffed hours. Shared numbers muddy call attribution and look like duplicate listings.
**A separate landing page per clinic**, and the profile links to that page — never to the homepage.
**Genuinely different page content**: the dentists who sit there, that clinic's timings, directions from a landmark people know, parking, the treatments available at that address only.

**No copy-paste locality pages** for areas where you have no clinic. `dentist in <every suburb>` templates are thin content, and they invite exactly the scaled-content problem that costs you the whole domain, not just those pages.

sections.h2: From map pack to filled chair — and what we guarantee
body: Google's profile performance report gives you calls, direction requests and website clicks. That's the top of it. The rest has to come from your side, and it's the part that turns SEO from an expense into an argument you can win with your accountant.

Track four numbers: calls from the profile, calls from the website (a tracking number, with your real line kept as an additional number on the profile), click-to-WhatsApp taps tagged with a URL parameter, and appointments actually attended. In Indian dental practice WhatsApp is frequently the largest channel and almost nobody instruments it.

A single clinic sits at the ₹40,000 a month end of our [SEO pricing](/pricing); a five-clinic group is ₹75,000 and up, because it's five profiles, five pages, five review programmes and a cannibalisation risk. [What local SEO costs](/cost/local-seo-cost) sets out the full range.

What we guarantee is not a position — nobody controls Google's index, and a dentist would never promise a specific outcome before seeing the X-ray. We freeze your trailing-90-day count of qualified enquiries from organic search on day one, calls and WhatsApp included. If we haven't beaten it in 90 days, we keep working free until we do. Three clients a month is the reason that's a real promise rather than a slogan.

callout.title: The realistic curve
callout.body: Profile and review work often shows movement in four to eight weeks — it's the fastest-responding surface in SEO. Treatment pages ranking for city-level cost queries take three to six months. If your agency's month-one report is all about blog traffic, the profile work isn't happening.

faqs.q: How do I get my dental clinic into the Google map pack?
faqs.a: Complete the profile properly (primary category, services with descriptions, real photos, correct hours, booking link), keep name, address and phone identical everywhere online, and build a steady review habit with replies. Then accept the geography: inside your 2–3 km ring this works, outside it you need locality pages on the site instead.

faqs.q: How many Google reviews does a dental clinic need to rank?
faqs.a: There's no threshold, and any agency quoting one is inventing it. What matters more than the total is the rate and the recency — a clinic adding six to ten a month with replies signals ongoing activity, which a static pile of 400 from 2021 doesn't. Never buy or incentivise them.

faqs.q: Should I publish my treatment prices on the website?
faqs.a: Yes, as a band with the reason for the range. Cost is what people are searching for, so the page that answers it captures the click and pre-qualifies the caller. Clinics that hide pricing get compared on nothing but distance, which is the one variable they can't change.

faqs.q: Is dental SEO worth it for a single-chair practice?
faqs.a: Often yes, and often without an agency. Get the Google profile right, ask every patient for a review, fix your site speed and write three honest treatment pages. That covers most of the available upside. Agencies earn their fee for multi-clinic groups, high-value implant and aligner competition, or when you have no time to run the review habit.

faqs.q: Do geotagged photos help a dental clinic rank on Google Maps?
faqs.a: No. Google strips EXIF metadata when you upload an image, so the location data never reaches the ranking systems. Photos still matter — a lot — because patients choose on them. Just not because of the coordinates embedded in the file.

faqs.q: Can dentists in India ask patients for online reviews?
faqs.a: Asking for genuine feedback is standard practice and generally acceptable. What isn't: writing reviews yourself, paying or incentivising for them, filtering to only happy patients, or replying with clinical details that identify a patient's treatment. Keep the ask neutral and the replies non-specific.
